theory: Faraday's law: the emf induced in a coil equals the rate of change of the magnetic flux linkage, $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d(N\Phi)}{dt}$.

A long solenoid with $n$ turns per metre carrying $I = I_0 \sin\omega t$ has a field $B = \mu_0 n I$ inside it. A search coil of $N$ turns and area $A = \pi d^{2}/4$ at its centre links $N\Phi = N\mu_0 n A I$, so the induced emf has peak value
$$\varepsilon_0 = N\mu_0 n A\,\omega I_0 = 2\pi f\,(N\mu_0 n A I_0)$$

At constant current the peak emf is proportional to the frequency, i.e. to the rate of change of flux: a graph of $\varepsilon_0$ against $f$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $2\pi N\mu_0 n A I_0$.
On the oscilloscope, $\varepsilon_0 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times$ (peak-to-peak height in divisions) $\times$ (volts/div). An a.c. ammeter reads the r.m.s. current, $I_0 = \sqrt{2}\,I_{\text{rms}}$.

apparatus.solenoid: Long solenoid with n turns per metre (on its label).
apparatus.coil: Search coil of N turns and diameter d, at the centre of the solenoid.
apparatus.generator: Signal generator with frequency display and amplitude control.
apparatus.ammeter: a.c. ammeter in series with the solenoid (reads r.m.s.).
apparatus.scope: Oscilloscope connected across the search coil.

safety: Keep the generator amplitude low enough that the solenoid does not warm up.
Switch the output off before changing connections.
steps: Connect the generator, ammeter and solenoid in series; connect the search coil to the oscilloscope. Record N, n and d.
Switch on and set the amplitude for a convenient current, e.g. 100 mA r.m.s.
Set the oscilloscope's volts/div so the trace fills as much of the screen as possible; read its peak-to-peak height Y in divisions.
Change the frequency. Re-adjust the amplitude until the ammeter reads the same current, then read Y again (changing volts/div if needed).
Repeat for at least six frequencies.
Work out ε₀ = Y × S / 2 for each, plot ε₀ against f, and use the slope to find μ₀.
tips: The current falls as the frequency rises (the solenoid's inductance): always bring it back to the same value before reading.
Use the smallest volts/div that keeps the whole trace on the screen.
Read the trace's top and bottom against the centre axis's fine marks (0.2 div).
references: Young, H. D. & Freedman, R. A. University Physics, ch. 29: Electromagnetic induction.
Physics Bench virtual laboratory — Faraday's law practical.

currentVaries.title: The current changed by {percent}% across your readings
currentVaries.detail: ε₀ ∝ f only at constant current. After each change of frequency, re-adjust the amplitude until the ammeter shows the same r.m.s. current.

peakToPeak.title: ε₀ is half the peak-to-peak value
peakToPeak.detail: Y is the peak-to-peak height. The peak emf is ε₀ = Y × S / 2.

offScreen.title: Some traces were taller than the screen
offScreen.detail: The screen is 8 divisions high, so a peak-to-peak height above 8 div cannot be read. Choose a larger volts/div.

tinyTrace.title: Some traces were very small
tinyTrace.detail: A trace under 2 divisions tall gives a large reading error. Choose a smaller volts/div so it fills more of the screen.
